sections.b: 1 Clement, the letter of the Roman church to Corinth (Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely in the last decade of the first century), tells the story at length. A single bird lives five hundred years in the lands around Arabia. Near death it builds a tomb of frankincense, myrrh and spices and dies in it; a worm born from its flesh grows into the new bird, which carries the bones of the old one to Heliopolis in Egypt and lays them on the altar of the sun in daylight, and the priests confirm from their records that five hundred years have passed (1 Clement 25:1–5). Clement tells it as fact and draws the lesson: if God shows a rising even through a bird, the Creator will surely raise those who served him (1 Clement 26:1). Herodotus had told an older form, with the parent carried in a ball of myrrh, and doubted it (Herodotus 2.73).

common: The phoenix is a legend; no such bird exists, and Herodotus already doubted the story (Herodotus 2.73).
uncommon: The phoenix could be taken as a familiar illustration rather than a claim of fact, but 1 Clement presents it as an observed event, checked against the priests' records (1 Clement 25:5).

claude.title: Claude's theory: a sign that keeps time
claude.body: Clement's version stresses the calendar: five hundred years, the priests' records, the bird arriving exactly on time. That fits his answer to the doubters of 1 Clement 23:3, who complained that God's promises were slow. The vine (23:4), the seasons (24:2) and the phoenix all say that God's works come on schedule. This is my reading of why the dates matter in his telling.

sections.b: Writing to the church that had heard Paul's 1 Corinthians 15, the Roman church gives three kinds of proof that the dead will rise. First, God has already raised the Lord Jesus Christ as the "firstfruits" (1 Clement 24:1). Second, nature: night sleeps and day rises; seed falls "dry and bare," breaks down and is raised by God's providence (1 Clement 24:3–5); and the phoenix rises from its own death (1 Clement 25). Third, Scripture: "And you will raise me up" and "I lay down and fell asleep; I woke up" from the Psalms, and Job's "you will raise up this flesh of mine" (1 Clement 26:2–3). Clement stresses the flesh that "has endured all these things," and later speaks of the "tomb and darkness" from which God first brought us into his world (1 Clement 38:3).

1 Clement gives a household code addressed to Christian men: show reverence for Christ, respect leaders, honor the older, train the young in the fear of God, and guide wives toward the good. The wives are to show pure character, a sincere and gentle will, a restrained tongue, and love given to all who fear God without taking sides; children are to learn humility, pure love and the fear of God (1 Clement 21:6–8). The order follows Titus 2 and 1 Peter 5:5, and the virtues are aimed at a church divided by arrogance and faction.

sections.h: 1 Clement 30–33: justified through faith, eager for good works
sections.b: The Roman church's letter to Corinth has three sentences on faith and works. "Be justified by works, not by words" (1 Clement 30:3). Christians "are not justified through ourselves ... or through works we have done in holiness of heart, but through faith," by which God Almighty has justified all from the beginning (1 Clement 32:4). And at once: "Are we to sit idle, stop doing good, and leave love behind? May the Master never let that happen" (1 Clement 33:1), with God's joy in his own works as the model. Lightfoot (1890) reads them as a "studied effort to keep the balance" between Paul and James: an emphatic statement "that men are not justified by their own works but by faith," at once balanced "by urging the importance of good works." The setting is an argument against pride: no one has glory "through themselves" (1 Clement 32:3).

1 Clement warns against being "double-minded" about God's promises and quotes an unidentified Scripture on the doubters who say the promises were old news to their fathers (1 Clement 23:2–3). It answers with the ripening vine and with God's faithfulness: "nothing is impossible with God except lying" (1 Clement 27:2). It then names faith as the way God "has justified all those from the beginning of time" (1 Clement 32:4), illustrated by Abraham, who "did righteousness and truth through faith" (1 Clement 31:2).

The Roman church's letter to Corinth quotes Job twice from the Greek. Job 19:26 becomes "you will raise up this flesh of mine, which has endured all these things," a proof of the resurrection (1 Clement 26:3). And Eliphaz's vision in Job 4:16–5:5, joined with Job 15:15, is quoted as "written" Scripture against the proud: no mortal is pure before the Lord, and those who live in houses of clay are crushed like a moth (1 Clement 39:3–9).

1 Clement 39:3–9 quotes Eliphaz's speech from Job 4:16–5:5 (in the Septuagint) with "it is written," to humble those who mock the church's order. The letter uses the friend's words for what they say rightly about human weakness, as Paul quotes Eliphaz in 1 Corinthians 3:19, though God tells Eliphaz at the end of Job that he did not speak rightly about him (Job 42:7).

1 Clement presents Jacob as a model of humility: he left his land because of his brother, served Laban, and was given "the scepter of the twelve tribes of Israel" (1 Clement 31:4). From him, the letter says, came the priests and Levites, the Lord Jesus "in his human descent," and the kings of Judah, all glorified "not through themselves ... but through his will" (1 Clement 32:2–3).

1 Clement says Isaac "knew with confidence what was going to happen, and he was gladly led up to be a sacrifice" (1 Clement 31:3), a willing sacrifice, as in 4 Maccabees 13:12, where Isaac "was willing to be slaughtered for godliness." Genesis 22 itself is silent about Isaac's mind.

"Why was our father Abraham blessed? Was it not because he did righteousness and truth through faith?" (1 Clement 31:2). The Roman church joins faith and deeds in Abraham, as Romans 4 and James 2 each stress one side, and adds the promise of offspring like the stars of the sky (1 Clement 32:2).

sections.h: 1 Clement 33: the Creator rejoices in his works
sections.b: 1 Clement retells creation to show that God loves good works: by his might he set the heavens in place, separated the earth from the water, made the animals, shut in the sea, and above all shaped the human being with his own hands as "the stamp of his own image" (1 Clement 33:3–4). Then he "praised" his works and blessed them (1 Clement 33:6). The Creator's joy is the "model to trace" for Christians (1 Clement 33:7–8).

sections.h: "The stamp of his own image" (1 Clement 33:4)
sections.b: 1 Clement says God formed the human being "as the stamp of his own image," using charaktēr, the word Hebrews 1:3 uses for the Son as "the exact stamp" of God's being, and quotes Genesis 1:26–27: "Let us make humankind in our image and likeness" (1 Clement 33:4–5).

1 Clement 36:1–6 calls Jesus Christ "the high priest of our offerings" and then follows Hebrews 1:3–13: the brightness of God's majesty, greater than the angels, then Psalm 104:4, Psalm 2:7 and Psalm 110:1 in the same order. Eusebius noted that Clement "gives many thoughts drawn from the Epistle to the Hebrews" and took it as proof that Hebrews was not recent (Church History 3.38.1–3). Lightfoot (1890) holds that the whole passage "is borrowed from the opening of the Epistle to the Hebrews." Shorter echoes stand at 1 Clement 17:1, 21:9 and 30:7.

sections.h: Christ "the high priest of our offerings" (1 Clement 36:1)
sections.b: Using the title only Hebrews gives Jesus in the New Testament, 1 Clement calls him "the high priest of our offerings, the protector and helper of our weakness" (1 Clement 36:1; also 1 Clement 61:3; 1 Clement 64:1). The letter does not say what the offerings are; it goes on to the Temple's order of high priest, priests, Levites and laypeople (1 Clement 40–41).

sections.h: The army and the body (1 Clement 37–38)
sections.b: To a church split by revolt, the Roman church offers two pictures. The army: not all are prefects or officers, but each in his own rank carries out the emperor's orders (1 Clement 37:1–3). The body: head and feet need each other, the smallest parts are necessary, and all "breathe together and share one submission" to keep the whole body safe; so "let our whole body be kept safe in Christ Jesus," each submitting to his neighbor by his gift (1 Clement 37:5–38:1). The strong care for the weak, the rich supply the poor, and no one boasts (1 Clement 38:2). The body picture is Paul's to the same church (1 Corinthians 12) and an old Roman lesson in concord (Livy 2.32).

sections.h: The Roman army as a model of order (1 Clement 37)
sections.b: Writing from Rome, the church holds up "the men who serve as soldiers under our commanders" as models of order, steadiness and obedience, with prefects, officers over a thousand, a hundred and fifty, and the emperor over all (1 Clement 37:2–3). The list joins Roman ranks to the biblical captains of Exodus 18:21. Army words run through the letter: "desert our post" (1 Clement 21:4), "deserts" (1 Clement 28:2).

sections.h: Scriptures 1 Clement quotes that no Bible has
sections.b: 1 Clement quotes as Scripture at least two texts found in no known book: the words on the double-minded and the vine, "Miserable are the double-minded ..." (1 Clement 23:3–4), also quoted in 2 Clement 11:2–4 as "the prophetic word," which Lake says "cannot be identified" though some think it comes from the lost Book of Eldad and Modad; and "Look, the Lord is taking for himself a nation from among the nations" (1 Clement 29:3), which Lake thinks may come "from some lost source." The Roman church's Bible at the end of the first century was not quite the same as any later canon.

1 Clement quotes Deuteronomy 32:8–9 from the Septuagint: the Most High "set the borders of the nations to match the number of the angels of God," and Jacob became the Lord's portion. The letter applies the second half to the church, God's "chosen portion" (1 Clement 29:1–2).

1 Clement makes humility the cure for the revolt at Corinth. It quotes "God takes his stand against the proud" (1 Clement 30:2), the form of Proverbs 3:34 that James and 1 Peter use, and lists "Brashness, self-will and recklessness" as marks of the cursed, "Forbearance, humility and gentleness" of the blessed (1 Clement 30:2, 30:8). It warns the humble not to praise themselves (1 Clement 38:2) and answers the proud who mock the church with Eliphaz's words: "what can a mortal do?" (1 Clement 39:1–9).

After the angels' "Holy, holy, holy" from Isaiah 6:3, joined with Daniel 7:10, 1 Clement calls the church "gathered together in one place in harmony" to "cry out to him earnestly, as if from one mouth" (1 Clement 34:5–7). The site's note on Isaiah 6:3 sees here a hint of the church's use of the angels' song in the Eucharist; the text itself asks for prayer with one voice.
